title: Can Your Insurance Company Make You Use Their Restoration Contractor?
excerpt: Adjusters recommend a preferred vendor and most homeowners assume it is required. In California it is not. Here is what the preferred-vendor arrangement actually is, and how to choose well.
author: Gallagher Restoration Team
imageAlt: Contractor and homeowner reviewing a restoration scope of work on a California property
metaTitle: Can Insurance Choose Your Restoration Contractor?
metaDescription: In California you choose your own restoration contractor — not your insurer. What preferred-vendor programs really are, and how to vet a contractor properly.

body.text: Within a few hours of opening a claim, most homeowners get a version of the same call: your adjuster has a restoration company they work with, and someone can be out today. The offer is convenient, it sounds official, and it is easy to hear as an instruction.
It is not one. In California, the homeowner chooses the contractor. Your insurer decides what it will pay for; it does not decide who performs the work on your property.
What a preferred vendor program actually is

Carriers maintain networks of restoration contractors — variously called preferred vendors, managed repair programs, or direct repair networks. Participating contractors agree to pricing terms, documentation standards, and volume commitments in exchange for a steady flow of referred work.

That arrangement is not inherently bad, and plenty of competent companies participate in it. But it is worth understanding what it is: a commercial relationship between the contractor and the party paying the bill. The contractor's ongoing referral volume depends on the carrier's satisfaction. When scope is disputed — whether a wall needs to come out, whether the ductwork is included, whether contents can be saved — that relationship is a real factor sitting on one side of the table.

items: You choose the contractor. Your insurer can recommend, and cannot require.
You are entitled to a written scope and estimate before work begins.
You are entitled to a copy of the adjuster's estimate.
You can request appraisal or invoke your policy's dispute-resolution provision if you and the carrier disagree on scope or amount.
You can file a complaint with the California Department of Insurance if you believe your claim is being handled unfairly.
Emergency mitigation does not require prior approval. You are obligated to prevent further damage, and reasonable mitigation costs are recoverable.

body.text: Anyone who works on your property must hold an appropriate California contractor license. The Contractors State License Board's guidance on [hiring a licensed contractor](https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Consumers/Hire_A_Contractor/) recommends verifying the license and photo ID before work begins, getting a written contract that details every aspect of the work, and being cautious with contractors who appear unsolicited after a disaster. You can verify any license number, including ours — CSLB #1061640 — on the CSLB website in under a minute.
Questions worth asking any restoration contractor

items: What is your CSLB license number, and are you IICRC-certified for this type of work?
Will you provide a written scope before starting, and will I get a copy of everything sent to my carrier?
Do you bill the carrier directly, and what am I responsible for beyond my deductible?
Who performs the work — your employees or subcontractors?
Will you document daily moisture readings and provide the log?
Do you handle both mitigation and reconstruction, or do I need a second contractor for the rebuild?
What happens if the carrier's approved amount does not cover the actual scope?

body.text: Question seven is the one that separates answers. A contractor who says the carrier's number will simply be the scope has told you how scope disagreements will go.
Where the friction usually shows up

rows: Determines whether the cavity dries properly
Moisture readings inside the cavity, documented
Daily moisture logs against a stated drying goal
Often the largest line on a fire claim
Documentation of residue found inside the system
Whether adjacent rooms are included for a match
Written flooring assessment and material availability
Inspection findings and moisture source documentation

body.text: Two things that are genuinely worth choosing for

First, response time. In water losses the category degrades with dwell time and drying gets longer and more expensive by the hour — the reasoning is laid out in our [restoration timeline guide](/news/how-long-does-water-damage-restoration-take). A local company with crews already in your county will be there before a dispatch queue routes someone from an hour away. We target 60 minutes on-site across [our five-county service area](/service-areas).

Second, documentation quality. The photographs, moisture maps, equipment logs, and written scope produced in the first 48 hours are the evidence your claim is settled on weeks later. That is the substance of [property damage management](/property-damage-management), and it is where a thorough contractor earns their place regardless of who referred them.
You can also decline the preferred vendor politely

You do not need a reason and you do not need a confrontation. "Thanks — I have already called a company I want to use, and they will be sending you their scope" ends the conversation. Then get your contractor and the adjuster talking directly. Most of what goes wrong on claims goes wrong because the homeowner ends up relaying technical information between two parties who should be speaking to each other.

items.q: Can my insurance company deny my claim if I use my own contractor?
items.a: No. Choosing your own licensed contractor is not grounds for denial. The carrier still evaluates the loss under your policy and pays what the policy provides. What can create friction is a scope disagreement — which is why a contractor who documents thoroughly and communicates directly with the adjuster matters more than who made the referral.

items.q: Do I have to get three estimates?
items.a: Generally no, though some policies or adjusters request them for reconstruction. For emergency mitigation it is rarely practical or advisable — the delay causes more damage than the comparison saves. For the rebuild phase, comparing bids is reasonable, provided you compare identical scopes rather than bottom-line numbers.

items.q: What if the insurance payment doesn't cover the full repair cost?
items.a: Discuss the gap with your contractor and your adjuster before work proceeds. Supplemental claims are routine when hidden damage is discovered after demolition begins, and carriers expect them. If the disagreement is about scope rather than discovered damage, most policies include an appraisal provision, and the California Department of Insurance accepts consumer complaints.

items.q: Should I sign an assignment of benefits?
items.a: Read it carefully before you sign. An assignment of benefits transfers your right to collect insurance proceeds to the contractor. It can streamline billing, and it also transfers leverage. Many reputable companies, including ours, bill carriers directly without requiring one — ask whether it is necessary before agreeing to it.
